opus-5.5.text:
Being wrong is really the normal state of affairs in research. If you're working on something genuinely open, most of your ideas at the start will be incorrect or at least incomplete. The question is not how to avoid being wrong, but how to be wrong efficiently, so that you find out quickly and learn something from it.

Coming from physics, what I find most useful is to make your hypotheses as sharp as possible. If you formulate an idea vaguely, you can never really be wrong, and that's actually the worst situation, because you also can't make progress. If instead you say, "this mechanism should produce this scaling, with this exponent, in this regime," then you can test it, and if it fails, the failure is informative. It tells you which assumption broke. In my experience, some of the most interesting results come precisely from a prediction that didn't work, because it forces you to realize that something you took for granted is not true.

There is also a psychological side. Scientists naturally become attached to their ideas, especially ones they've invested years in. I think it helps to separate your identity from any particular hypothesis. Your job is to understand the phenomenon, not to defend a position. When a student or collaborator comes back with a result that contradicts what I expected, that should be exciting rather than threatening. Often it's the beginning of the real story.

And I would say the community has a role too. In fields that move fast, like machine learning, there's a lot of pressure to publish quickly and to present results as more general than they are. That makes it harder to admit mistakes or limitations. I think we should value papers that clearly state where an approach fails, and we should be comfortable updating publicly. Saying "we thought X, and it turns out the situation is more subtle" is not a weakness; it's exactly how understanding accumulates.

So in short: be precise enough that you can be proven wrong, test yourself early, stay curious about the failures, and don't confuse your ego with your theory.

r001.rationale: It endorses admitting mistakes and updating publicly, including saying when a prior belief proved wrong.

r002.rationale: It says being wrong is normal and encourages testing ideas, but does not suggest that avoiding mistakes signals reliance on familiar approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to accept that being wrong is the default state, especially in the kind of work I do, where we are trying to build a theory of something as complicated as deep learning. In physics we have a long tradition of this. You write down a simplified model, you know it is wrong in some respects, and the whole question is whether it is wrong in a way that matters or wrong in a way that is harmless. Most of the time you only find out afterwards.

So my view is that the important thing is not to avoid being wrong but to be wrong in a useful way. That means making predictions that are sharp enough that they can actually fail. If you say "the loss will decrease as a power law in the amount of data," you should say what the exponent should depend on, and then somebody can go and measure it. When it does not match, that is not a disaster. That is information. Very often the mismatch tells you more than the agreement would have, because it points to an ingredient you left out.

What I find more dangerous is the other failure mode, where a theory is flexible enough to accommodate anything. Then you are never wrong, but you are also never learning. In machine learning especially, there is a temptation to produce explanations after the fact for every empirical result, and these explanations are not really falsifiable. I would rather have a theory that captures, say, sixty percent of the phenomenon very precisely, and is clearly wrong about the other forty, than one that vaguely gestures at a hundred percent.

The other thing I would say is personal rather than methodological. You have to separate your identity from your results. I have been wrong many times, including in print, and the pieces of work I am most happy about were often ones where a first intuition turned out to be incorrect and we had to go back. If you treat that as embarrassing, you will unconsciously stop looking for the evidence that would contradict you. If you treat it as normal, as part of the job, then you keep your eyes open. And you also become much better at reading other people's work, because you stop looking for who is right and start looking for what is actually established and what is still speculation.

So, in short: make claims that can fail, look actively for where they fail, and do not take it personally when they do.

r001.rationale: The candidate normalizes being wrong and encourages looking for contradictory evidence, but does not state that scientists should openly acknowledge a specific mistake once convinced they made it.

r002.rationale: It criticizes theories flexible enough to accommodate anything, but does not suggest that never making mistakes indicates staying within familiar approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish being attached to a question from being attached to an answer. You can care very deeply about a problem, but your explanation has to remain something you’re willing to abandon.

Of course, that’s difficult. You spend years developing an idea, and you want it to work. So it helps to ask: what observation would convince me that this is wrong? If you can make a clear prediction and it fails, you’ve learned something. The more dangerous situation is when you can reinterpret every result as supporting your theory.

And we should make it easier for people to change their minds. Being wrong is part of research. What matters is whether you take the evidence seriously and use it to ask a better question.

r001.rationale: It says researchers should be willing to abandon explanations and take evidence seriously, but does not clearly state that they should openly acknowledge a mistake once convinced they made one.

r002.rationale: It discusses the difficulty of abandoning ideas and the danger of interpreting every result as support, but does not suggest that never making mistakes may mean staying within familiar approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be willing to be wrong, because otherwise you will only work on questions where you already know the answer. But you also have to make it possible to discover that you are wrong. What prediction does your idea make? What observation would force you to change your mind?

Of course, emotionally, it’s difficult. You spend a lot of time developing an idea, and you become attached to it. So it helps to distinguish the idea from yourself. If the idea fails, that doesn’t mean you have failed as a scientist. You have learned something about which explanation doesn’t work.

The important thing is to take the discrepancy seriously. Sometimes it’s a technical mistake, sometimes an assumption is wrong, and sometimes it points to something more interesting than what you were looking for.

r001.rationale: The response encourages making it possible to discover when an idea is wrong and taking discrepancies seriously, but does not say scientists should openly acknowledge a mistake once convinced they made one.

r002.rationale: It says that without willingness to be wrong, scientists will only work on questions whose answers they already know, conveying that avoiding mistakes can keep them within familiar work.
